questions.question: Historically, what was the early common belief about the shape of the Earth and the movement of the stars and Sun?
options: The Earth was flat, and the Sun and stars revolved around it.
The Earth was a sphere orbiting a stationary Sun.
The Earth was flat, but only the Moon moved around it.
The Earth was a cylinder, with the stars remaining perfectly still.

questions.question: Until which century did most people believe that the Earth was situated at the very centre of the universe?
options: The 12th century
The 16th century
The 19th century
The 20th century

questions.question: Which technological development has been most crucial in providing the observational evidence needed to understand the universe?
options: Navigational compasses
Hot air balloons
Telescopes
Barometers

questions.question: What is the angle at which the Earth's axis of rotation is tilted?
options: 12.5 degrees
23.5 degrees
45.0 degrees
90.0 degrees

questions.question: In which direction does the gravitational force of a large celestial object, like a planet or star, pull other objects?
options: Towards its outer atmosphere
Parallel to its equator
Towards its centre
Away from its magnetic poles

questions.question: How does the mass of an object affect the strength of its gravitational pull?
options: Greater mass results in a stronger gravitational pull.
Greater mass results in a weaker gravitational pull.
Mass only affects gravity if the object is spinning rapidly.
Mass has no effect on the strength of gravitational pull.

questions.question: What is the primary effect of the Earth's gravitational pull on the Moon?
options: It pushes the Moon further away into deep space.
It causes the Moon to rotate much faster on its own axis.
It heats up the Moon's surface to create volcanic activity.
It constantly changes the Moon's direction, keeping it in orbit around the Earth.

questions.question: What happens to rays of light when they hit a flat surface directly face-on compared to hitting it at an angle?
options: They are more spread out face-on.
They are less spread out face-on.
They reflect completely and do not heat the surface.
They are absorbed only if the surface is highly polished.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a star?
options: A small solid rock that reflects light from nearby planets
An extremely large sphere of hot gas that gives out light
A cold, dense cloud of dust that absorbs light
A ring of ice particles orbiting a central planet

questions.question: Which of the following represents the correct collection of objects orbiting the Sun in our solar system?
options: 8 planets, dwarf planets, and smaller objects like asteroids
12 planets, 3 stars, and a single large black hole
Only 4 planets and a ring of icy comets
Millions of stars and several galaxies

questions.question: What occurs in the Northern and Southern hemispheres during the month of December?
options: Both hemispheres experience summer due to being closest to the Sun.
The Northern hemisphere is tilted away from the Sun (winter), while the Southern hemisphere is tilted towards it (summer).
The Northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun (summer), while the Southern hemisphere is tilted away from it (winter).
Both hemispheres experience winter because the Earth's tilt is temporarily reduced to zero.

questions.question: Why do countries located near the Equator not experience distinct summer and winter seasons?
options: They remain close to 'face-on' to the Sun all year round.
They are shielded from solar radiation by the Earth's magnetic field.
The Earth's axis does not tilt in the equatorial region.
High cloud cover blocks all variations in sunlight throughout the year.

questions.question: What is a light-year, and why is it used by astronomers?
options: The time it takes for the Earth to orbit the Sun, used to measure planetary ages.
The distance light travels in one year, which is suitable for measuring vast distances in space.
The speed of light in a vacuum, used to calculate the temperature of stars.
The intensity of light emitted by the Sun in twelve months, used to measure solar energy.

questions.question: In the universe, how are stars distributed?
options: They are evenly spaced in a perfect grid across empty space.
They are found in groups called galaxies, which contain billions of stars.
They are all clustered around a single central super-star.
They are found only within the boundaries of our solar system.

questions.question: How long does it take for the Earth to complete one full orbit around the Sun?
options: 24 hours
27.3 days
365.25 days
1000 days

questions.question: How long does the Moon's orbit around the Earth take, and what visible phenomenon does this explain?
options: It takes about 24 hours, explaining day and night.
It takes about 365.25 days, explaining the change of seasons.
It takes about 27.3 days, explaining why the Moon appears to change shape.
It takes exactly 12 hours, explaining the rising and falling of high tides.
